verses.text: It was decided that we would sail to Italy. Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to an army officer named Julius. He belonged to the Emperor's Regiment.
We got on a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail to ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius was kind to Paul and let him visit his friends, so they could give him what he needed.
From there we put out to sea again. The winds were against us, so we sailed on the sheltered side of Cyprus.
We crossed the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, and landed at Myra in Lycia.
There the officer found a ship from Alexandria that was sailing to Italy, and he put us on board.
We sailed slowly for many days and had a hard time reaching Cnidus. The wind would not let us go on, so we sailed on the sheltered side of Crete, past Salmone.
We moved along the coast with difficulty and came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.
We had lost a lot of time, and sailing had become dangerous, because it was already after the Day of Fasting. So Paul warned them.
He said, "Men, I can see that this trip will be dangerous. We will lose the ship and its cargo, and we may even lose our lives."
But the officer listened to the pilot and the owner of the ship instead of listening to Paul.

The harbour was not a good place to stay for the winter. So most of the men decided to sail on and try to reach Phoenix, and stay there for the winter. Phoenix is a harbour in Crete that faces both southwest and northwest.
When a gentle south wind began to blow, the men thought they could do what they had planned. So they pulled up the anchor and sailed along the coast of Crete, close to the shore.
But soon a very strong wind, called the Northeaster, came down from the island.
The ship was caught by the storm and could not sail into the wind. So we gave up and let the wind carry us along.
We passed the sheltered side of a small island called Clauda. With great difficulty we pulled in the lifeboat.

After the men had lifted it on board, they tied ropes around the ship to hold it together. They were afraid of hitting the sandbanks near Syrtis, so they lowered the sea anchor and let the ship be driven along.
The storm was beating so hard against us that the next day the men began throwing the cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship's equipment overboard with their own hands.
For many days we could not see the sun or the stars, and the storm kept raging. At last we gave up all hope of being saved.

The men had gone a long time without food. Then Paul stood up in front of them and said, "Men, you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete. Then you would have avoided all this damage and loss.
But now I beg you to be brave. None of you will lose your life. Only the ship will be lost.
Last night an angel came and stood beside me. He was sent by the God I belong to and serve.
The angel said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. And God has given you the lives of everyone sailing with you.'
So be brave, men! I trust God that it will happen just as he told me.
But we will run aground on some island."
On the fourteenth night, we were still being driven across the Adriatic Sea. At about midnight, the sailors felt that we were getting close to land.
They dropped a weighted line and found that the water was about thirty-seven metres deep. A little later they measured again and found it was about twenty-seven metres deep.
They were afraid we would hit the rocks. So they dropped four anchors from the back of the ship and prayed for daylight to come.
The sailors tried to escape from the ship. They lowered the lifeboat into the sea, pretending they were going to drop some anchors from the front of the ship.
But Paul said to the officer and the soldiers, "If these men do not stay on the ship, you cannot be saved."
So the soldiers cut the ropes that held the lifeboat and let it fall away.
Just before dawn, Paul begged everyone to eat something. He said, "For fourteen days you have been waiting and worrying, and you have not eaten anything.
So I beg you to eat some food. You need it to stay alive. Not one hair on your heads will be lost."
After he said this, Paul took some bread and thanked God for it in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat.
They all felt braver, and they ate some food too.
There were two hundred and seventy-six of us on the ship.
When everyone had eaten enough, they made the ship lighter by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not know what land it was. But they saw a bay with a sandy beach, and they decided to run the ship onto the beach if they could.
So they cut the anchors loose and left them in the sea. At the same time they untied the ropes that held the steering oars. Then they raised the front sail to the wind and headed for the beach.
But the ship hit a sandbank where two currents met, and it ran aground. The front of the ship stuck fast and would not move, and the back of the ship was being broken to pieces by the pounding waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim away and escape.
But the officer wanted to save Paul's life, so he stopped them. He ordered everyone who could swim to jump overboard first and swim to land.
The rest were to follow, holding on to planks or pieces of the ship. And so everyone reached land safely.
